prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that the clock transition is unperturbed, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B018 with Katori and Ye as my preferred single-part configuration, and the first round made my reasons more precise, not different. The central idea is a statement about atomic structure: for a chosen wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, so atoms can be held tightly in a lattice, in the Lamb-Dicke regime, without Doppler or recoil shifts and without perturbing the transition. That idea is what lets one interrogate thousands of neutral atoms at once and so combine ensemble statistics with the systematic control that before was available only for a single ion. This is the answer to the chair's first question: the comb is the ruler that reads out an optical clock, and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems. Neither contains the magic-wavelength lattice, and neither explains why the neutral-atom clock reaches its stability. The physics, and not only the performance, is distinct. The achievement has also been tested the way I trust: the same architecture works in Sr, Yb and other species in Tokyo, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, and clocks have been compared across laboratories. The scientific consequences, resolving the gravitational redshift across millimetres, bounds on drifts of constants, and a many-body clock whose interactions are controlled, say something about the quantum system and not only about a better instrument. On credit I see Katori for the proposal and the first strontium clock, and Ye for taking the accuracy, coherence and many-body operation to the record level. Five members independently name the same pair, and no member proposes a different B018 configuration. I would want the citation to say lattice clock and magic wavelength explicitly so the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is on the page.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection has not disappeared, and Kroll rightly reminds me that Olsson and I, both from the atomic side, may underweight how colleagues from other fields hear it. If a majority reads the lattice clock as a downstream use of combs and ion control, the prize would be criticised as a second-generation refinement. Ye's association with Hall and the comb strengthens that reading unless the citation is written carefully. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so a part of the impact is still prospective. Credit also has edges that two names cannot cover: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups made real contributions, and I cannot from these files separate exactly how much of the 1e-18 milestone belongs to the Ye group and how much to collaborators. Finally, if the committee wants a result that surprises us about nature, B018 is a refinement of understanding more than a surprise, and I accept that this is a judgment and not a fact.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the physics, and not only the performance, of the lattice clock is distinct from the combs and ion control, and applies a rule that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to a later and better realisation, which makes Ye's share the open question.
responses.response: I agree that the physics is distinct, and I would put it in one image: in an ion clock one particle sits in a trap and the trap field is zero where the ion sits, and in a neutral-atom lattice the atoms sit where the field is strong, so the clock transition is only unperturbed because of the magic-wavelength condition. That is a new design principle with consequences for the many-atom statistics, and it is not a faster comb. On Ye I think your rule is met if the citation is written around the invention and development of the clock, which is how I phrased it. Katori's proposal and first Sr clock are the original step. Ye's group did not merely tune it: its systematic work, cryogenic and blackbody-shift control, long coherence and the many-body treatment of interactions turned a demonstration into a clock at the 1e-18 level and defined what the clock can resolve. I accept that this is a development credit and not an original-concept credit, but the prize has often recognised both in one citation.

responses.point: Johansson says that the 2005 and 2012 prizes are a reason to state precisely what is new (magic-wavelength Lamb-Dicke trapping of many atoms and the resulting statistical gain and 1e-18 systematics), and that the redefinition of the second is a possible argument that the application is ahead of the discovery.
responses.response: I accept your wording and have rewritten my citation to carry it. On the redefinition, I would separate two questions. Whether the second is redefined is a decision by metrology bodies about practicality and continuity, and it does not depend on whether the physics has been understood and reproduced, which it has. The accuracy has been established and compared between laboratories, and waiting for the SI decision would make the prize hostage to a process unrelated to the discovery. My one concession is that if the redefinition were being delayed because the evidence of reproducibility were thin, I would change my mind; I have no sign that this is the case, but I cannot verify the current record numbers myself and I support Pearce's request that expert reviewers confirm them.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B038, the gamma-ray burst afterglows, as a clue from nature that turned a thirty-year mystery into a field, but he concedes that the optical counterpart and redshift credit may sink it on attribution, and he asks whether the committee wants a second precision-measurement prize after 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I defer to you and Pearce on astrophysics and I find the scientific case for the burst afterglows compelling in the way you describe, because it is a discovery about nature and that is what I value most. My difficulty is the same one you name: the localisation by BeppoSAX, the optical counterpart and the redshift involved different teams and instruments, and I do not see how Costa, Frontera and Kulkarni fit them without excluding people who clearly mattered. Your concern about a third precision-measurement prize is fair, but I would count it as an argument about what the clock is, not about whether it is a repeat. The earlier prizes honoured a ruler and the control of single particles; the lattice clock introduces a new trapping principle. If the expert reports on attribution produced a clean, eligible set of names for B038 I would take it seriously as a rival, and I would be glad to see Pearce's recusal question settled first.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B044) for Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, argues that an unresolved pairing mechanism does not undermine a robust phenomenon (citing the cuprates), and keeps B034 only as an alternative.
responses.response: Your cuprate analogy is fair and it softens my position. The prize does not need the mechanism if the phenomenon is robust and reproduced, and the match between the continuum-model band structure and spectroscopy is the kind of quantitative theory-to-measurement link I trust. I did ask in round 1 what is settled enough to write into a citation, and your own citation answers it reasonably: the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states. My remaining hesitation is the one you share, that the first experimental authors and precursor theory are omitted, and that the field is moving to moire TMDs. I still prefer B018, because its picture is stable and quantitatively understood, but I have kept B044 as my first alternative and would not oppose it if the lattice clock case fails to hold.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the theory of defect-mediated 2D melting (B012) on grounds of maturity and clean attribution, acknowledges its thin opening support and the 2016 overlap, and suggests testing a two-part configuration that pairs B012 with B018 or B008.
responses.response: I take B012 seriously as mature physics with clean attribution, and I accept your point that first-order melting in some systems qualifies universality. I do not support a two-part prize here, for the reason you note yourself: the three-name limit would force an unacceptable cut. Pairing B012 with B018 would give at most one or two names to each part, and for B018 the pair Katori and Ye is already the minimum, so I would lose Ye or Katori to make room, and I think that damages the case that is cleanest. I also agree with your own remark that B018 has a clearer before and after in the laboratory. I would stay with a single part.

uncertainties: Whether the colleagues who see overlap with 2005 and 2012 find the citation wording on the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation sufficient, since Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson have not yet said so.
I cannot verify the current record uncertainties and inter-laboratory comparisons from these files and would ask for expert confirmation before the final ballot.
Whether Ye's share is judged an original contribution or a development, and whether the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups should alter the credit.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second, which I think it should not.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I have no known collaboration with Katori or Ye. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund attosecond group and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, where Andreas Wallraff (B008) is based, and I know of no connection to him. B008 is only an alternative for me. I note Johansson's stated recusal on B008, Kroll's link to the Hall environment, and Pearce's possible recusal on B007 and B038, and I do not think any of them bears on B018 for me.
